title: Top-k KV Eviction Can't Know What It Threw Away
hook: Deterministic cache eviction is blind by construction: nothing you kept reveals how much error the deletions caused. Sample randomly instead and the leftovers become a statistical certificate.
key_points: The authors prove no serving-time estimator of deterministic top-k eviction error can be consistent.
Evicted values can be altered so everything the server retains is unchanged while true attention-output error grows arbitrarily.
Poisson-sampling the tail at known inclusion probabilities restores identifiability; one logit offset applies the Hajek correction inside the softmax.
A survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set yields a per-step error certificate at 0.97 empirical coverage and no accuracy cost.
Seven claims were pre-registered and three lost — notably, output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate does.
What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73-0.75 vs 0.47-0.54) and schedules recomputation.
content_html: Long-context serving leans on KV-cache eviction: score each token's importance, keep the top k, delete the rest. The uncomfortable question is how much accuracy that costs on any given request. This paper's first result is that with deterministic eviction, you fundamentally cannot tell.
extra_html:
An impossibility, then a fix

The proof is a construction: you can alter the evicted values so that everything the serving system still holds is bit-identical while the true attention-output error grows without bound. Since the retained set is all a server can see, no serving-time estimator of that error can be consistent — deterministic eviction "cannot know what it destroyed." Randomization restores identifiability. Poisson-sample the tail at known inclusion probabilities, apply the Hájek correction with a single logit offset inside the softmax, and a standard survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate — 0.97 empirical coverage, at no accuracy cost.

Pre-registered, and partly wrong

The evaluation is unusually honest: seven claims registered in advance, three lost. Question-aware eviction at 25-50% budgets turns out to be nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate does; and certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution — the certificate separates cache-induced failures from failures the model would have had anyway (AUC 0.73-0.75, against 0.47-0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. The author's own summary: randomization buys attribution, not prediction. Xie, arXiv 2026.

related.title: The KV Cache & Continuous Batching
related.hook: Generating one token reuses every prior key and value - that growing cache is why LLM inference is memory-bound, and continuous batching is how servers fight back.

related.title: ReFreeKV: Threshold-Free KV Cache Compression
related.hook: Most KV-cache pruning needs a hand-tuned budget threshold per input — pick wrong and performance craters. ReFreeKV adapts the budget on the fly instead.

related.title: The Draft Isn't Free at a Million Tokens
related.hook: Speculative decoding assumes the draft is cheap. At million-token context the draft head reads the entire KV cache every step — and can end up slower than no speculation at all.

related.title: PagedAttention / vLLM: Efficient LLM Serving
related.hook: LLM serving wastes huge amounts of GPU memory on the attention cache. PagedAttention borrows an OS trick — paging — to recover it and serve many more requests at once.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't a serving system estimate the error caused by deterministic top-k KV eviction?
flashcards.back_html: The evicted values can be changed so that everything retained looks identical while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily — so no consistent estimator exists from the retained set.

flashcards.prompt: What does randomized (Poisson-sampled) eviction buy, according to the paper's own conclusion?

choices.text: Attribution — telling cache-induced failures apart from inherent ones — rather than prediction of failure
Better raw accuracy at the same cache budget than top-k eviction
A reliable early-warning signal that beats output confidence at predicting failures

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors are blunt: output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate. The certificate's value is separating cache-caused failures from inherent ones (AUC 0.73-0.75 vs 0.47-0.54).

flashcards.prompt: What makes this paper's negative results credible?
flashcards.back_html: Seven claims were pre-registered before the experiments and three were lost, including one of the paper's own proposed uses — certificate-gated budget escalation, which added nothing.
